title: You Think Repeating Notes Locks In Memory, Yet One Deep Question Quintuples Recall
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — Craik & Lockhart (1972) / Craik & Tulving (1975): Why Deep Meaning Triples Memory Without Even Trying to Memorize, grounded in Fergus I.M. Craik, Robert S. Lockhart (1972) (Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior). Empirical findings show that before 1972, students and textbooks believed a seductive lie: keep a word spinning inside Short-Term Memory long enough by repeating it over and over, and it automatically 'transfers' into permanent Long-Term Memory.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how primary visual cortex, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that at the University of Toronto in *1972 (JVLVB), Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart demolished that pipeline myth: memory durability is NOT determined by which box an item sits in or how many times* you mutter it (Type I Maintenance Rehearsal), it is a direct byproduct of HOW DEEPLY you process its meaning (Type II Elaborative Processing).

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Fergus I.M. Craik, Robert S. Lockhart (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-5371(72)80001-x
- Fergus I.M. Craik, Michael J. Watkins (1973). The role of rehearsal in short-term memory. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-5371(73)80039-8
- Michael W. Eysenck (1978). Levels of processing: A reply to Lockhart and Craik. British Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1978.tb01645.x
